The product worked. The launch didn’t.

We had spent months building something people said they wanted. The demos went well. Early feedback was encouraging. We took that as a signal to launch.

Then almost nobody came back.

Looking back, we had asked plenty of questions about the product and very few about the behavior it needed to replace.

“Would you use this?” gave us enthusiasm.

“Show me how you handle this today” would have shown us the friction: existing tools, familiar routines, and a problem that wasn’t urgent enough to justify switching.

The lesson I took away: interest is a starting point, not proof of demand.

Now, before investing in a launch, I look for a concrete commitment. Will someone make time for a pilot? Bring in a teammate? Use the product on a real task without a reminder?

A failed launch is expensive. So is mistaking polite encouragement for evidence.

I lost a deal I’d already counted toward our quarter.

We had a strong champion, positive feedback on the demo, and a proposal that seemed to check every box. In our forecast meeting, I called it “very likely.”

Then the buyer chose to stay with their current process.

When I asked what we’d missed, our champion said: “The team liked your solution. We just couldn’t agree that changing was worth the disruption.”

I’d coached my rep on how to beat the competition. I hadn’t helped them understand what it would take for the customer to make a change.

That loss changed how I run deal reviews.

Alongside “Why would they choose us?” I now ask:

• What happens if they do nothing?
• Who will carry the work of switching?
• Have we heard those people’s concerns directly?

I also had to own my part. My confidence had made it harder for the rep to raise doubts.

A sales manager’s job includes making room for bad news while there’s still time to act on it.

I wish I’d learned that before we lost the deal.

When I managed a remote team for the first time, I thought my job was to make myself available.

So I kept my calendar open, answered messages quickly, and added check-ins whenever something felt unclear.

But the same questions kept coming up. Decisions stalled until I came online. My availability had become part of the workflow.

The lesson: being easy to reach doesn’t replace giving people enough context to move forward.

I started writing down what success looked like, who owned each decision, and when to ask for help. After meetings, we captured the decisions and the reasons behind them.

It took more effort upfront. It also meant fewer interruptions and less waiting across time zones.

I still value being available. But now, before wrapping up a conversation, I ask: “Does everyone have what they need to take the next step without me?”

Subject: Connecting store inventory discrepancies to their financial impact

Hi [First Name],

When inventory and sales records disagree across hundreds of stores, Finance often inherits the reconciliation work: explaining margin variances, validating inventory balances, and determining which discrepancies need attention before close.

I’m Elena Park at Clearcount. We help retail finance teams reconcile store-level inventory against sales data so they can identify discrepancies, understand their financial impact, and give store operations a clear path to resolution.

Clearcount brings inventory movements and sales activity into a consistent view by store, SKU, and reporting period. Starting with opening inventory, it accounts for receipts, transfers, returns, and recorded adjustments, then compares the expected ending balance with reported inventory. Matching those movements against sales helps surface exceptions such as timing differences, missing transfers, duplicate transactions, and unexplained shortages.

For Finance, the value is a traceable explanation of what changed, where the records diverged, and which exceptions warrant investigation. Your team can focus on material discrepancies instead of rebuilding spreadsheets and requesting supporting records from individual locations.

As an illustrative customer example, consider a national apparel retailer whose stores repeatedly show inventory shortages after promotional weekends. Reconciliation could reveal that some discrepancies reflect delayed sales postings, while others stem from transfers recorded at the sending store but missing at the receiving location. Separating those issues would help Finance avoid treating every variance as shrink and route each exception to the right owner.

I’d welcome the chance to learn how your team handles this today and discuss where Clearcount could fit into your existing close and inventory-control processes.

Would you be open to a 20-minute call next week? We could use one representative store reconciliation to make the conversation concrete and assess whether a broader evaluation would be worthwhile.

Best,
Elena Park
Clearcount

Shutting down my first startup taught me lessons I wish I’d understood when I started.

The hardest one: effort and progress are different things.

When you care deeply about what you’re building, it’s easy to treat every release, customer conversation, and late night as evidence that you’re getting closer. But activity only matters if it changes the fundamentals: Do people need this? Will they pay for it? Can you reach them consistently?

I also learned that persistence needs checkpoints.

“Keep going” is useful advice until it becomes a reason to avoid an uncomfortable decision. I wish I’d defined clearer milestones earlier—and decided what we would do if we missed them. Making those decisions while you still have options is much easier than making them when you’re exhausted.

Another lesson: ask for help before you’ve polished the story.

I sometimes felt I needed to arrive with answers before talking to people who could help. In hindsight, sharing the uncertainty would have made those conversations more useful. A candid “Here’s what isn’t working” gives someone a chance to challenge your assumptions.

And finally, closing a company deserves the same care as starting one.

There are commitments to honor, difficult conversations to have, and people whose time and trust deserve respect. Handling those responsibilities thoughtfully matters, even when there’s no exciting announcement at the end.

I’m still disappointed it didn’t work. I can appreciate what I learned without pretending that learning was the outcome I wanted.

Next time, I’ll test the riskiest assumptions sooner, pay closer attention to what customers do, and set firmer limits on how long we operate without convincing evidence.

For now, I’m grateful to everyone who gave the company a chance—and taking the time to understand what happened before deciding what comes next.

Five years of managing a remote engineering team taught me that distance is rarely the hardest problem. Ambiguity is.

The biggest improvements came from changing how we worked together:

1. Write to make decisions easier.

We started documenting decisions because people kept missing context. Over time, I learned that a useful document doesn’t need to be long. It needs to explain the problem, the tradeoffs, the decision, and who owns the next step.

That small habit reduced repeat conversations and gave engineers more room to move without waiting for someone to come online.

2. Build trust before you need it.

A quiet Slack channel can mean focused work. It can also mean someone is stuck and uncomfortable asking for help.

Regular one-on-ones, informal conversations, and admitting my own mistakes helped me understand the difference. The goal was to make it easier for people to say, “I don’t understand,” or “This deadline is slipping,” while there was still time to respond.

3. Make ownership explicit.

Our most frustrating delays often happened between people: a review waiting on an unnamed reviewer, a decision everyone assumed someone else would make, a handoff with no clear recipient.

Naming an owner, agreeing on the expected outcome, and setting a check-in point prevented a surprising amount of confusion.

I still get these things wrong. Under pressure, it’s easy to skip the written context or assume everyone knows who’s doing what.

After five years, those are the habits I keep returning to. They make the work clearer and the team easier to be part of.

One lesson I learned from a failed product launch: people saying “that sounds useful” isn’t the same as people choosing to use it.

We spent a lot of time getting the product ready and too little time finding out where it fit into someone’s day. Launch day came, we shared the link, and… mostly crickets.

That stung. But it changed how I approach new ideas.

Now I ask people to walk me through how they handle the problem today. I learn more from watching them work than from hearing whether they like a pitch.

Wish I’d learned that a little earlier.

My first year as a manager changed how I think about doing good work.

As an individual contributor, I could usually measure my impact by what I finished. As a manager, I had to learn to see progress in other places: a clearer decision, a teammate taking ownership, a difficult conversation that happened before frustration built up.

A few lessons I’m taking into year two:

Clarity takes more effort than I expected. Something can feel obvious in my head and still be unclear to the team. Explaining the goal, the tradeoffs, and what success looks like is work I need to make time for.

Listening means leaving room for an answer I didn’t anticipate. When I jump straight to advice, I can miss the actual problem—and the chance for someone to work through it themselves.

Feedback gets harder the longer I wait. Being direct and being kind can happen in the same conversation. Avoiding discomfort usually just passes it to someone else.

Delegation requires patience. Giving someone ownership means accepting that their approach may look different from mine, and resisting the urge to step in too quickly.

And trust grows through small commitments: following up, admitting uncertainty, and doing what I said I would do.

I’m still learning how to balance support, accountability, and space. Going into year two, I want to ask better questions and make fewer assumptions.
